title: Leaders Who Cant One Day See Themselves Working for Any of Their Team Members
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article uses the exercise of imagining which team members could someday be a leader's own boss as a diagnostic for developmental effectiveness. It argues that great leaders take pride when the people they've coached surpass them, viewing it as proof of good development rather than a threat, while insecure leaders resist the possibility because their self-worth is tied to being irreplaceable. The piece recommends leaders run this mental exercise honestly on their current team and treat an empty list as a signal to either coach more aggressively or examine their own ego.
points: Whether a leader can imagine reporting to a former direct report is a useful self-assessment exercise.
The best leaders view being surpassed by those they developed as a career highlight, not a threat.
Insecure leaders tie their self-worth to seniority and resist developing people past their own level.
An empty list of potential future-bosses should prompt honest self-examination, not just team review.
quotes: As team members develop and grow as contributors and leaders in their own right, they often develop strengths, skills, and experience far above those of the team leader.
Good leaders relish developing and nurturing a team member to such a high level of skill and polish that they get promoted above them.
The very job of leadership is to attract, retain, and develop talent to such a high level as to make the leader superfluous.
If the list is empty, a leader must look in the mirror and ask why.
Self-importance can be debilitating for anyone, but especially for leaders. True learning and leadership require people to suffer an injury to their self-esteem at times.
